stops.name: Fountain Court, the last day and the death
stops.campa: Blake works at the Dante drawings until his strength gives out, then turns to Catherine, in tears at his bedside, and asks her to stay just as she is so that he may draw her portrait once more, for she has ever been an angel to him; he finishes it, lays down his tools, and begins to sing. His friend George Richmond, sent for, later writes that he died in a most glorious manner, saying he was going to the country he had all his life wished to see, and just before the end his countenance grew fair, his eyes brightened, and he burst out singing of the things he saw in Heaven.
stops.quote: Stay, Kate! Keep just as you are — I will draw your portrait — for you have ever been an angel to me.
stops.quote_source: George Richmond's account, recorded in Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 36

stops.name: Bunhill Fields, the burial
stops.campa: Five days after his death, William Blake is carried to the Dissenters' burying ground at Bunhill Fields and laid in unconsecrated ground not far from his brother Robert, in a grave he shares, unmarked at the time, with strangers above and below him, as was the custom of the poor. Catherine, faithful past the end, tells visitors in the years remaining to her that William still comes and sits with her of an evening and advises her on her work. No stone marks the exact spot for a century; when one is finally raised, it will carry his own words: Jerusalem's wall.
